It starts back around the year 600 A.D. when Christian missionaries arrived in England with their Roman alphabet. They found the Anglo-Saxons, who spoke a Germanic language, with different kinds of sounds like [th] and [x] that Latin didn't have. So scribes came up with their own ways to write them. Over a long time everyone finally settled on the gh for the [x], but there is no [x] in thought! Anymore. The pronunciation changed over hundreds of years. 2403:
Transcription

It starts back around the year 600 A.D. when Christian missionaries arrived in England with their Roman alphabet. They found the Anglo-Saxons, who spoke a Germanic language, with different kinds of sounds like [f] and [j] that Latin didn't have. So scribes came up with their own ways to write them. Over a long time everyone finally settled on the gh for the [j], but there is no [j] in thought! Anymore. The pronunciation changed over hundreds of years. [j] turned to [f] in words like cough and enough, or disappeared entirely in words like though or thought.
2404:
Transcription

As those changes were getting underway, the printing press was invented and that was great for the spread of written English, but unfortunately it was also great for the spread for the spellings that printers had decided on before the pronunciation changes already in progress were complete.
2405:
Transcription

Other pronunciation changes that happened over this time period where the loss of certain sounds at the beginning of words and an almost complete overhaul of the entire vowel system of English known as the great vowel shift.
2406:
Transcription

So for the most part, the answer to "why do we spell it that way?" is either "because we used to pronounce it that way" or "because that's how they did it in French."
2407:
Transcription

In the late 1500s, English spelling had stabilised well enough, but some Renaissance scholars who were all fired up about classical Latin and Greek decided not to leave well enough alone.
2408:
Transcription

They decided words like receipt, salmon, indict, and debt, needed to put their Latin roots and better display, so they purposely added letters that no one had ever pronounced in English.
2409:
Transcription

That's what happened with colonel. We borrowed it from French, along with a lot of other military vocabulary, in the 1500s. Back then they said it and spelled it as coronel. Later English scholars started translating old Italian military treatises, where it was collonelo. Time goes by, and wouldn't you know it, people are spelling it the Italian way and pronouncing it the French way.

Screening of passengers and luggage inside the terminal has been a mainstay, but increasingly the worry is also what happens on the entire grounds of an airport.
3000:
Transcription

DON EHRENHOLZ: We put into place a number of additional security measures yesterday, in light of the Istanbul events. (=after what happened in Istanbul)
3001:
Transcription

DON EHRENHOLZ: And I’m not at liberty to tell you what those  [the new security measures] are... that would give the bad guys some advantage.
3002:
Transcription

The goal is to create as many obstacles as possible for would-be terrorists.
3003:
Transcription

Other countries have taken extraordinary security measures. Many of them have learned their lesson the hard way.
3004:
Transcription

In Moscow, in 2011, a suicide bombing in the arrivals terminal killed 37 people. Now travellers go through security checks before they even get to the airport buildings.
3005:
Transcription

In 2007, two men in a jeep packed with propane canisters tried to smash into Glasgow airport. Concrete barriers prevented them from killing people inside.
3006:
Transcription

So airports are constantly evolving and trying to stay one step ahead of the threats, increasingly forgoing a one-size-fits-all security approach in favour of a more tailored system depending on the airport and the intelligence gathered by security officials.

 For centuries aboriginal people in Australia have used native plants, seeds and fruits to make medicines and remedies. (It means that they still use them, because we use the present perfect for situations that started in the past and continue in the present).
3008:
Transcription

The results could see traditional bush remedies on pharmacy shelves or beauty stores around the world. [...] And if the results are positive these old bush goods could be marketed beyond the northern territory.
3009:
Transcription

These women are rangers from Wadeye, 450 km. southwest of Darwin and the largest aboriginal community in the northern territory.
3010:
Transcription

NARRATOR: For centuries their ancestors have been using native plants to make home remedies, medicines, insect repellent, even beauty products. And it’s a tradition that’s still alive.
ABORIGINAL WOMAN: ...and we go back to ranger base and we boil it and we make soap, shampoo and lip balm.
3011:
Transcription

NARRATOR: Researchers say the early results are promising.
RESEARCHER: “This is a secret... I cannot disclose much of this information, but we are really optimistic on some of the positive outcomes because we know that there is a wealth of chemicals in all these indigenous plants.”
3012:
Transcription

And the women from Wadeye aren’t waiting to see what the science has to say. They’re confident their goods can do the job and they’ve opened up a little store in one of Darwin’s most popular markets to sell their wares to tourists and locals alike.
3013:
Transcription

And if the local interest is anything to go by, there’s a definite place on world markets for the ancient products. (It means that if we take the local interest as a reference, the ancient products will sell well on world markets, which means that there is a local interest.)
3014:
Transcription

They were bagged alive and ready for export, but these pangolins never reached their final destination, which was probably China, where they are eaten and used in medicines.

Transcription

Thailand is the hub of Southeast Asia's illegal wildlife trade. Its poorest borders provide an attractive route to lucrative markets further away.
3019:
Transcription

NARRATOR: Inside the animal section, all sorts of endangered species can be found on display. Traders are sensitive to publicity but using a hidden video camera it's plain to see how easy it is to buy an endangered animal, like the star tortoise, found mainly in India and Sri Lanka. Police seem almost defeated; they conduct regular raids and arrests but more often than not they are outwitted by the sellers.

The challenge of a life-support system that can operate for years without resupply is daunting. The cost will be high and the hurdles immense. But the challenge is so exciting, it seems certain that some will try it, and quite likely that some will die trying.

I don't speak those languages. In fact, very few people do. They're used only by a handful of people and all those languages are in danger of extinction.
5533:
Transcription

There are more than 7,000 languages spoken in the world today. But about a third of those have fewer than 1,000 speakers and according to UNESCO more than 40% of those languages are in danger of extinction. In fact, every fortnight, one of the world's languages disappears forever.
5534:
Transcription

When you say dead language, many people think of Latin. But, Latin actually never died. It's been spoken continuously since the time of the Caesars, but it changed very gradually over 2,000 years until it became French, Spanish, and other romance languages.
5535:
Transcription

True language death happens when communities switch to other languages and parents stop raising their children to speak their old one. When the last elderly speaker dies, the language is unlikely ever to be spoken fluently again.
If you look at this chart which measures the world's languages in terms of their size and their state of health, you can see that most languages are ranked in the middle. English, like just a few other dominant languages, is up at the top left-hand corner. It's in a really strong state. But if your language is down here in the bottom right-hand corner of the graph, like Kayapulau from Indonesia or Kuruaya from Brazil, you are are in serious trouble.
5536:
Transcription

In the bad, old days governments just banned languages they didn't like. But sometimes the pressure is more subtle. Any teenager growing up in the Soviet Union soon realized that whatever language you spoke at home, mastering Russian was going to be the key to success. Citizens of China, including Tibetans, as well as speakers of Shanghainese or Cantonese, face similar pressure today to focus on Mandarin.
5537:
Transcription

Just one language has ever come back from the dead: Hebrew. It was extinct for two millennia but Jewish settlers to Palestine in the early 20th century spoke different languages back in Europe and they adopted Hebrew on their arrival as their common language. It became Israel's official language when the country was fully established in 1948 and now has seven million speakers.

My husband and I moved to the Scilly Isles six years ago. We were on holiday on the biggest island here, St Mary’s. We loved it! It was safe and quiet, and the beaches were beautiful with soft sand and clear sea. I didn’t want to go home! One day we went on a trip to another island, called Bryher. There, we saw a pub for sale. I said to my husband, “Why don’t we buy that pub and live here?” He said yes!

I work there now, as a gardener. My husband works at a hotel. Tresco is the second biggest island in the Scilly Isles, but it’s less than 3 square kilometres. St Mary’s, the biggest island, is 6 and a half square kilometres. Over 1500 people live on St Mary’s, but about 200 people live on Tresco. Less than a hundred live on Bryher. I think I’d feel lonely there!

We’re actually very different. He’s quieter and more serious than me. He hates sports and prefers reading and learning about history. I prefer science and I’m much more active.

I live in a small town called Farley. It’s in the south west of England. It’s near the mouth of a river, about six miles from the coast. There aren’t any beaches in the town itself, but there are some not far away, about eight miles.

5936:

Back then, coal, food, wood, cloth and all kinds of things were brought here by sea. That’s why there are so many small houses beside the river. They were built about 130 years ago for the port workers and fishermen. Now they are empty for most of the year. They were bought as second homes.

The houses are better maintained now too.

‣ After a preposition, we use -ing.
‣ To review the use of infinitives and gerunds, go to Grammar » A2 » Infinitives and gerunds – verb patterns

4 Correct answer: lots of

‣ We use a lot of or lots of (more informal) before both plural (countable) and uncountable nouns.

‣ To review quantifiers, go to Grammar » A2 » much, many, little, few, some, any – quantifiers

‣ This sentence is passive. In a passive sentence, the subject is the receiver of the action, NOT the doer.
‣ To review the passive voice, go to Grammar » A2 » Present and past simple passive: be + past participle

6 Correct answer: do you have

‣ The verb have in have to is not an auxiliary verb. Use do/don’t, does/doesn’t, did/didn’t in questions and negative sentences in present and past.

7 Correct answer: safer

‣ One-syllable adjectives take -er/-est in the comparative and superlative forms.

8 Correct answer: anyone

‣ We use anything, anybody/anyone, anywhere in negative sentences and questions.
‣ We use nobody/no one, nothing, nowhere in sentences with an affirmative verb.
‣ To review this grammar topic, go to Grammar » A2 » Something, anything, nothing, etc.

9 Correct answer: should

‣ This is a first conditional sentence.
‣ In the first conditional, the verb in the if clause is present and the verb in the main clause is future..
‣ In the main clause, we can also use may, might, can, must, should instead of will. In this case, we use should because we are giving advice.
‣ To review First conditional sentences, go to Grammar » A2 » First conditional and future time clauses

10 Correct answer: might

‣ We use might, might not when we think something is (not) or will (not) be true, but we aren’t sure.

‣ We use who to talk about people, which to talk about things or animals and where to talk about places.

‣ When we use a verb after when, once, as soon as, before, after or until to talk about the future, we have to use this verb in the present tense (NOT future). We use the future in the other part of the sentence.

But with that money, I could buy a nice big house in the country. I could decorate it nicely, get some nice furniture and hire a cleaner and a gardener. Then I could get a car – a new one, not a second hand one, a dog and some horses. I think that would cost all my money, though, so I would still have to work! But that’s okay. I enjoy my job. I wouldn’t quit that for all the money in the world.

LOUISE: What I’d do with a million pounds? Well, first I would quit my university course in finance – it’s really boring! With a million pounds, I wouldn’t have to worry about studying something sensible and getting a safe job. I’d study something creative, like jewellery making or fashion design. I’d get myself a little studio with lots of really good equipment. I’d hire some nice people to work with, and we’d work if we felt creative, or just relax and chat and drink tea! We wouldn’t make much money, but that doesn’t matter. I wouldn’t spend all the million pounds. I’d save some so that I didn’t have to worry about earning more.

‣ We use the when we are talking about specific things or people (the table next to the door, the man behind you, the person who they were talking about, etc.).
‣ To review the use of the article, go to Grammar » B1 » A(n), the, no article
6918:
‣ Must only has a present form, so for all other verb forms (past, future, perfect forms, infinitive, etc.) we need to use have to.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Have to, must, should – obligation, prohibition, necessity, advice
6919:
‣ We use each other or one another when person A does something to person B, and person B does something to person A.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Reflexive pronouns – myself, yourself
6920:
‣ We use the past perfect with to talk about states or situations that had started earlier in the past.
‣ To review the narrative tenses, go to Grammar » B1 » Past simple, past continuous, past perfect.
6921:
‣ Third conditional: If/unless + past perfect (,) would have/could have/might have + past participle of main verb.
‣ We don’t use a comma when the main clause comes first and the if clause comes second.
‣ To review the third conditional, go to Grammar » B1 » Third conditional – past unreal situations.
6922:
‣ We use a to + infinitive after too + adjective, or after too much/many + noun: There are too many people to enjoy the scenery.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Gerund or infinitive – do, to do, doing.
6923:
‣ We can say either A or B to mean one person/thing or the other.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » both, either, neither – quantifiers.
6924:
‣ In a question tag, we must use the same auxiliary verb as in the main clause (in this case, have).
‣ If the auxiliary verb is positive in the main clause, it should be negative in the question tag and vice versa.
‣ To review question tags, go to Grammar » B1 » Question tags – aren’t you? don’t you?
6925:
‣ We can use (not) to/so as (not) to/in order (not) to + infinitive to express purpose.
‣ We can use for + noun to express purpose (NOT for + verb).
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Clauses of contrast, purpose and reason.
6926:
‣ We can say that someone is obsessed with something or someone.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Adjective + preposition – dependent prepositions.
6927:
‣ We use since and from + a starting point. They are used to mark the beginning of something: an action, a state or an event.
‣ The difference is that we normally use since with present or past perfect tenses and from with other verb tenses.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » For, since, from – What’s the difference?
6928:
‣ Use number + hyphen (-) + singular noun in compound adjectives.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Compound adjectives with numbers: ‘a two-day trip’
6929:
‣ If you hang out in a place or you hang out with someone, you spend a lot of time in that place or with those people.
‣ To review phrasal verbs, go to Grammar » B1 » B1 Phrasal verbs 2 – Exercises and explanation.
6945:
‣ We use the present perfect to talk about past recent events.
‣ In questions, the present perfect is: have + subject + past participle of the main verb.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Past simple or present perfect?

6968:
‣ We use another or the other + singular noun, and other + plural noun.

6969:
‣ The form used to only has a past form. To talk about present habits, we can use usually or normally with the present simple tense.

‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » usually, used to, be used to, get used to.
6970:
‣ We use the active voice when the subject (before the verb) does something, and we use the passive voice when something happens to the subject.
‣ In this sentence, the subject is 'Children under 12', and something must happen to them (an adult must accompany them).
‣ After must (or will, can, should, might, etc.) we always need an infinitive. The passive infinitive is the infinitive of be (be) + past participle (accompanied).
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Passive verb forms.
6971:
‣ We use must when we are sure, or quite sure, that something is true. You must be wrong.= 'I'm sure you are wrong.'
‣ We don't use can as a modal verb of deduction.

6972:

‣ Second conditional: If/unless + past  (,)  would/could/might + infinitive.
‣ To review the second conditional, go to Grammar » B1 » Second conditional – unreal situations
6973:
‣ We use to + infinitive after too + adjective, or after too much/many + noun: There are too many people to enjoy the scenery.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Gerund or infinitive – do, to do, doing
6974:
‣ We can use all/both + (the/my/etc.) + noun.
‣ We can use all/both + of the/my/Tom’s + noun, or all/both + the/my/Tom’s + noun (without of) but we cannot use both/all of + noun.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » all, both – quantifiers
6975:
‣ I will go to the festival. (direct speech) ⇒ I would go to the festival. (reported speech).
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Indirect speech – reported speech.
6976:
‣ People is a plural countable noun (one person, two people, three people, etc.)
‣ We use (a) little, a bit of or much before uncountable nouns and (a) few before countable nouns.
‣ To review quantifiers, go to Grammar » B1 » much, many, a lot, little, few, some, any, no – quantifiers
6977:
‣ We use had better to give strong advice or to tell someone (including ourselves) what to do.
‣ The short form of had better is ‘d better.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Had better… It’s time…
6978:
‣ We use whose as the possessive form of who (whose friend= 'the friend of whom').
‣ Whose can be used for people and things.
‣ To review relative pronouns, go to Grammar » B1 » Defining and non-defining relative clauses.
6979:
‣ We say spend money on something or invest money in something.
‣ To review this grammar lesson, go to Grammar » B1 » Verb + preposition – dependent prepositions.

PRESENTER: America's first polio case in nearly a decade was discovered in Rockland county, New York, this spring. There are now believed to be hundreds of cases in the area. Polio was one of the most feared diseases in the US in the early 1950s. It caused more than 15,000 cases of paralysis in a year. That all changed in 1955
6981:
Transcription

PUBLIC SERVICE ANNOUNCER: Today, the tragedy of paralytic polio can be prevented in individuals protected by all three recommended doses of polio vaccine. However, there are still millions of Americans who have received only one or two of the doses, or none at all. These are today's potential victims. You can avoid all the expense, suffering, and heartache that paralytic polio causes if you make use of the vaccine that is now available.

PRESENTER: That was a public service announcement from the 1950s urging Americans to get the new polio vaccine.
6982:
Transcription

PRESENTER: My dad was born in 1938 before the vaccine was available. And he contracted polio as a young child. The disease left him with a severe limp, and he suffered from related muscle weakness later in life. I saw the effects of polio on my dad's life. And some of you shared your own memories of how the disease shaped your lives.
6983:
Transcription

WOMAN: My parents cried when the polio vaccine came out. We were eight children, and very vulnerable. We were not allowed to swim in municipal swimming pools in the summer. My family, we collected... uh... dimes for the March of Dimes Polio Research. My best friend's mother had polio and '...' '...' with her legs, she needed crutches all her life.
6984:
Transcription

PRESENTER: For 40 years, the US has been polio-free. How do we make sure polio doesn't return to the US? And what should you be doing to protect yourself and your loved ones? Joining us now is Dr. Jose R. Romero. He's the director of the CDC's National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases. Dr. Romero, welcome to the program.

DR. ROMERO:  Thank you, Ms White. Thank you very much. And thank you for sharing that personal anecdote with us.

PRESENTER: Of course. Now, this case in Rockland county, New York, was the first documented polio case in the US, as I said, in nearly a decade. Why are we seeing new cases appear now?

DR. ROMERO: It has to do with the fact that immunization rates are lower in some communities and others. And so, with an incursion of polio... uh... poliovirus that can cause... um... paralysis, those populations are extremely vulnerable. This is a disease, as you've mentioned before, that can be prevented by a vaccine that has... uh... we have experience with for over 50 years. It's safe and effective. So people can take... uh... take control of this... and prevent this disease by taking the vaccine.
6985:
Transcription

PRESENTER: Now, the man who contracted the virus was unvaccinated against polio. Here's a clip, a clip of chief medical advisor, Dr. Anthony Fouci, speaking to NPR yesterday about vaccination rates in the county where the outbreak started.

DR. FAUCI: Polio is 99% preventable by vaccines. If you look at certain places in New York, such as in Rockland County, only about 60% of the children are vaccinated and in some sections of the county, as few as 37% are vaccinated. That's unacceptable. You've got to get the children vaccinated. 

PRESENTER: How do these rates square up with the rest of the country?

DR. ROMERO: So, they're much lower. So, overall, the United States... uh... we're about 94 to 95% vaccinated. Um... and even in New York state, it's 93, 94% of the population has antibodies for polio from vaccination.

7288:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: Is salary a deciding factor when choosing a job?
TOBY: I remember at school years ago, we always used to say that the amount of money you earn is unimportant and that it's better to have an interesting job as long as you get a fair wage. Well, that's just it, isn't it? When I started looking at how much these interesting jobs pay and the number of unpaid hours you are expected to do, it's just not enough to live on. So, I've changed my tune now. I'm not prepared to work for next to nothing.
7289:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: Would you be willing to work longer hours if you were asked to?
TOBY: There's only so much I'm prepared to do. I have friends who work all the hours god sends, thinking all those extra hours will earn them recognition in the company and get them a promotion. I'm not convinced that it gets them anywhere, and they don't have much of a life outside of work. I'd rather maintain a decent work-life balance.
7290:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: How important is flexibility?
TOBY: Very important. I'm sure everyone would agree. It's impossible to raise children, see a doctor or care for your elderly relatives with most jobs. I'm sure lots of people would love the chance to choose their hours or work from home. I'm lucky in that way. I know a lot of people would like to be in my shoes.
7291:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: Are you happy with your vacation time?
TOBY: I get 21 days' paid vacation each year. It's… er… a bit less than I got at my last job, which is frustrating, cos travelling's the thing I most want to spend my money on. What's more, the people with families always get in there first when booking time off, whereas I always leave it to the last minute. It means I sometimes don't get the chance to go away when I want to, or for as long as I want.
7292:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: How long is your commute?
TOBY: It takes me two hours to get to and from work in the car. I have to travel during rush hour, of course, and it takes twice as long as it does at any other time of day. Thankfully, I'm working two days a week from home now, so that's saved me a lot of time and fuel costs. These days I just put on some podcasts and relax, and I don't get as frustrated with the slow traffic and bad driving these days as I used to.
7293:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: What can you tell us about the importance of relationships in the workplace?
TOBY: For me, the one thing that can make or break a job is the people you work with. You can have the most boring job, but if you are working with fun, easy-going people, the day whizzes by. It's the luck of the draw, though. You can't force it. Those team-building days they sometimes put on won't help to bridge a divide between people who just can't work well together. There are people I clash with at work. I just try to avoid them as much as I can.
7294:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: How secure do you feel your job is at your company?
TOBY: Of course, everyone is concerned about job security. I don't think anyone can take it for granted that their job is secure. There has been company restructuring a couple of times at my company, but I've managed to escape being laid off. I'm always on tenterhooks, though, and I'm always keeping an eye out for other companies in the area which I could work at if I do get let go.

Fortunately, I warned her before it was too late. Scammers attract people with bargain prices, so she didn’t lose much.

Feedback

I was already familiar with the puppy scam then. We’d learnt about scamming during internet safety classes at school, though I heard about the puppy scam elsewhere. It was mentioned in an online video about the different ways scammers get money out of people.
7356:
Feedback

Scambaiting involves engaging scammers in conversation. When they ask you to do something, you act a little stupid by asking lots of questions or making mistakes. It’s frustrating for them, but they stay on the line patiently because they think they will get money out of you. I don’t think you can be a scambaiter unless you are pretty sociable, as you have to talk to people for a long time.
7357:
Feedback

I scambait first and foremost because I want to help people recognise scams, and although most viewers of my videos are young, I’m sure the content they learn passes on to other family members. It’d be nice if I actually helped to get a scammer arrested, but there are just too many scammers for police to deal with. But as long as I am wasting a scammer’s time, that person can’t be scamming someone else. I also get a bit of income from the adverts that go out on my videos.
7358:
Feedback

Some scambaiters go too far, though, when creating entertainment by punishing the scammers. I saw one video in which the scambaiter convinced a scammer that he had a well-paid job for him in Lagos. The guy used all his money to travel to the capital of Nigeria, and when he got there, there was nothing for him. For the scambaiter and the viewers, that was all a big joke. For that poor guy in Africa who was trying to earn a living by any means, it was a real situation and it could have been dangerous.
7359:
Feedback

But I hope the conversations I have with them go some way in helping people understand the lives of people in poor countries and the things they have to do for cash.
7360:
Transcription

I remember when we left school, we were all eager to meet up at a reunion ten twenty years down the line. We said we'd want to see how we've changed, but let's face it, we were all looking forward to a chance to brag about our achievements. That doesn't appeal to me anymore, nor do I really care about hanging out with people from my past. I've kept up with the ones I really care about. I was more curious about the place itself. It had always been so old-fashioned. I wondered if it had remained that way or moved on.
7361:
Transcription

At first, the atmosphere was rather awkward. I paired off with a close friend, Emily, and we updated each other on life. Around us, some people were squealing with joy as they met long-lost friends and reminiscing, while others who had come and then realised they didn't know anyone very well were making polite small talk in a very restrained way. Neither of those options was attractive to me, but Emily eventually said that we should mingle, so I did.
7362:
Transcription

Fortunately, then one of the organisers announced that we were going to play a game. We had to write down our memories and guess who had written them. You'd think it would fall flat because most people barely knew each other, but actually, it was a good ice-breaker. After that, people were no longer pretending to be interested in each others' careers and families. We knew what to talk about – you know, events, classrooms, teachers and so on, and it brought home what we had in common; and also what set us apart, because people had responded differently to what was basically the same experience.
7363:
Transcription

Later on, we had a tour, and the headteacher gave us an update on the school's facilities and the latest news. She spoke proudly of the new history block, the computer laboratories and the school's excellence and recognition in music. What struck me, though, is how little had changed. Despite all these modern updates, the school ethos is still to help teenagers excel in activities that are somewhat outdated rather than teaching the kinds of skills that are valued today.
7364:
Transcription

Naturally, that led to a discussion about what the school had done well and what it should have done differently. Interestingly, we all used to think the school was far too strict, but now I appreciate that that approach taught me discipline. I also have always thought that the school had too few options. It prepared everyone for the academic route to university, and to be fair, it did that very well. Pretty much everyone got in. But as far as preparation for the workplace goes, there was none of that. It seemed they were just passing the buck.
7365:
Transcription

Although it wasn't the best evening of my life, the reunion was a good opportunity to reflect. After all, the school taught me to be hard-working and capable, and I've always been aware of the benefits that has brought me. I'm pleased to have met up with old classmates too. It was interesting to see how our shared education has shaped everyone differently, so I'll definitely keep in touch with them. I can't say my memories of school are any more positive. It'll take more than one evening to change those, but all in all, I'm glad I went.

Transcription

Lots of people dream of working in the movie industry. I guess they think the excitement of the movie will become part of their life, and yeah, it's true, a career in the movies is very different from being in an office all day, but let me tell you, it's not a bed of roses by any means. First of all, you have to accept that you'll constantly be scraping around for work. You might get a great job for a few months, but then that's it. I've been in the business for eight years, but even now, there's no promise of a new contract after one ends. There are loads of talented, enthusiastic and qualified people in the same position.
7422:
Transcription

Well, I can't speak for the people who are high up, but if you are in a junior role, like me, you spend a lot of time standing around, waiting for something to happen. But then, when something needs doing, it needs doing right there and then. So, you can't just chill out with your workmates or wander off. You need to be acutely aware of what's going on and ready to spring into action the moment you are needed. No one wants to be kept waiting because they can't find you.
7423:
Transcription

Yeah… the people… There are some fascinating, creative characters working in the movies, but let's face it, there are some difficult personalities too. Creative people tend not to be very logical, practical or organised. The successful ones are, but you will have to work with a lot of scatterbrains before you can work with them. Literally everyone is bad-tempered and stressed, and you will have to deal with people at their worst. I know I have snapped at people myself. But to survive in the industry, you can't take things personally. Not everyone can handle it, though. I've known many highly talented people who have left because they'd had enough of all the drama.

Well, at the same time, when you are working on a film, you are part of a close-knit team for anything up to three months, and you'll get to know each other really well. And yeah… For me, that's one of the things I like about it. There's no … kind of… pretence. Politeness and respect go out of the window very fast. And instead, you are free to be yourself, and for those few weeks, you are accepted as part of a community, warts and all. That said, you have to put up with everyone else's quirks and bad habits. You need an open mind.

Transcription

The first time you ever work on a film shoot, you will have no idea what's going on. There's a kind of language of slang words and jargon on set that is incomprehensible to anyone else. You don't pick it up at film school, for sure. But you need to pick it up because if someone comes along and asks you to do something, they won't have time to explain what they mean. If you can't figure it out for yourself, they'll think you're useless, roll their eyes and ask someone else nearby.

Transcription

JENNIE: When I went to university, my parents were… they were very generous really. They offered to pay for my first year's accommodation in halls of residence, fully catered. It was fine by me, cos it saved me worrying about it. So, I applied for a place, and I was given a room in an all-female hall, which I was a bit annoyed about, cos that wouldn't have been my first choice, to be honest. But when I rang up the accommodation and asked if I could change, they said they couldn't, or wouldn't, so I went along with it. It wasn't a particularly nice place, as I was on the basement level down this rabbit warren of corridors, and it was really noisy and too hot for my liking. A few other girls moved into other accommodation, but… well, it didn't seem worth the hassle. The place was convenient walking distance from my department, and I didn't have to think about meals. I just had to see to my laundry. I knew it wouldn't be forever, so I stuck it out. I kept myself to myself most of the time. I dare say people thought I was a bit odd, sitting by myself at mealtimes, but I could come and go as I pleased, so it suited me.
7530:
Transcription

JOSEPH: For my first year at university, I moved into a shared house. I'd chosen that over halls of residence because I thought it'd be quieter. It was just across the road from my department, so I thought it would be ideal. But I knew from the second I arrived that I was going to hate it. There were six people in the house altogether, and the others were all so noisy that I couldn't bear it. They had no consideration for anyone. They kept their music on really loud, had parties on any day of the week, and smoked like chimneys, so the place stank. If I asked them to keep it down so I could sleep or study, they would be really rude and sometimes aggressive. And they left the place in a real mess, and I wasn't prepared to wash up and clean the bathroom for them. But sometimes I had to, just to be able to prepare a meal. It got to the point where I couldn't take it any longer, and I went home. I almost quit the course, but my mum helped me to find somewhere else to spend the rest of the academic year. I lodged with an old lady called Gladys, who made me a cake each week. That was far more preferable in my eyes and it wasn't far from campus either.

7532:
Transcription

BEN: I couldn't wait to move away from home and experience the university lifestyle. My parents were all worried about whether I'd be able to look after myself properly, but I said, 'Sure, sure, I'll be fine!' and paid no attention to them. I was in a self-catering hall of residence, right in the middle of the campus, next to the student bar. It was nice. It had a private bathroom and a shared kitchen, which was cleaned once a week by a cleaner, poor woman. Looking back, I feel really sorry for her because we left the place in a real mess. I can't remember washing up once. But then, I mostly ate microwave meals because I couldn't be bothered to cook. As for laundry, I didn't do that either. I just went home every now and then with a huge bag of dirty washing and handed it to my mum. If I ran out of clean clothes, I just bought more. I ran up huge credit card bills and had to get a second student loan. But I wouldn't change a thing. The people along my corridor were a great laugh. We had some mega parties. I guess we weren't very mature, but who wants to be, at university?

My classmates hated me, of course. That didn't bother me, to be honest. Doing well in exams gave me confidence and a sense of pride, although I confess, I also felt I was better than everyone else, which I now realize is not true. I simply have a better aptitude for that way of learning, I suppose. Now, I work with people whose grades aren't even close to mine, and they do better than me in the office. Although I haven't seen any real financial benefit from taking exams, they have made me a disciplined person who values knowledge, and I still take them now for the hobbies I do in my spare time. It was my decision to end it. I just couldn't see us staying together long-term. He took it quite badly. In an ideal world, I would have moved out to give him some space, but we just couldn't afford it.
8566:
Transcription

I was living in a shared apartment with my boyfriend, Adam, and another couple, Sarah and Luke, who were our friends. We'd just signed a rental agreement to stay there for another six months when we broke up.
8567:
Transcription

Fortunately, there was a little storage room in the apartment, and I moved into that, giving him the master bedroom that we had shared before. There wasn't enough space in it for all my clothes – I have quite a lot of them – so I had to keep going in his room, but I did my best to give him some space. It wasn't easy, for sure.
8568:
Transcription

I knew he hoped that we would get back together,...
8569:
Transcription

I knew he hoped that we would get back together, and one time, after I'd had a rough day at school and was really stressed, I turned to him for comfort. It was just so easy to slip back into old habits, and he was there, and I knew he could give me the support I wanted. But I shouldn't have done that. It gave him false hopes, and things were tense for a while after that.
8570:
Transcription

We had agreed that we wouldn't date anyone else while we were living in the same apartment, and I kept my word, but it didn't quite go according to plan. You see, there was a guy at school who I got to know, and there was an instant attraction between us. I was honest with him. I told him I was living with my ex and that it wouldn't be possible to take things further for a while, and he was fine with that. But of course, we flirted, and we often met up for coffee, and then I told Sarah, the friend who we were living with, about him.
8571:
Transcription

And one day, we were gossiping about him in the kitchen, and she was asking me all these questions, and I was chatting away, and then Adam walked in. He'd been in the living room and overheard every word. I hadn't realized he was there. It was very awkward. He didn't speak to me for a while after that, and that weekend, he went out partying and brought a girl home. I'm sure he didn't have any feelings for her. It was just him showing he didn't care or pretending to show it.
8572:
Transcription

After that, I kept out of his way as much as possible. When we were together, I was distant and polite. And he avoided me, too. It wasn't easy, for sure, trying to cook and do the laundry when the other one wasn't in the room. It was hard on our friends, too. Gone were the days when we'd hang out in the living room watching TV with takeout and a bottle of wine, playing board games together, or watching a movie.
8573:
Transcription

The apartment was very tense. I stayed until the six months was up and then moved out.
8574:
Transcription

Really, I should have moved out sooner, as it really hurt my friendship with Sarah – or with all of them, really. She hasn't reached out to me since then. And I'm sure Adam was glad to see me go. I guess it was natural that we couldn't just end things immediately after being close, but while we were living together, neither of us could move on.

INTERVIEWER: When did you decide to live in a campervan?
DEB: We moved into a campervan about a year ago when my partner Nick got a job as an auditor. It meant he was away from home for three or four days each week in different parts of the country. I hardly saw him. That was when we had the idea to move into a campervan. That way, I could go with him.
8576:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: Where do you travel?
DEB: On a normal week, we travel to wherever Nick has to work, usually a town or city somewhere. We park up in a campsite or, failing that, a quiet lane where locals won't mind a van being parked for a few days. We aren't really city people, so at the weekends, we head somewhere else in that general region to do some hiking or bike riding and explore a bit.
8577:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: Do you have a job?
DEB: Moving into the campervan meant I had to leave my own job, but that didn't matter; I had a rather dull office job at the time. I had this idea. I would paint landscapes and sell my artwork as we travelled around. I wouldn't need to earn much because our costs would be much lower. But I soon got bored and frustrated when my pictures didn't sell, and the van got cluttered with kit. I missed doing something useful. So, I'm doing an online accountancy course. Once I'm qualified, I'll be able to work online from here in the van.
8578:
Transcription

DEB: I write a blog, too. Initially, I thought I'd write all these exciting posts about how great it was to be free and maybe get some money from advertising. But that got harder too, because, frankly, moving from place to place where you don't know anyone is tough, especially when it's wet and cold, and you are stuck in a van with the same person. Finally, I stopped pretending life was great and wrote the truth and used it as a way to get things off my chest. I doubt if anyone reads it, to be honest. I haven't told my friends about it.
8579:
Transcription

INTERVIEWER: What is hard about living in a van?
DEB: You see, there are lots of things to think about when you are in a van. Where will you get things delivered? How much stuff can you buy? Where will you do your laundry? These things used to be real issues for us, and it still saddens me that I don't have my piano, sewing machine, or all that cooking equipment that I used to have in my flat, and I can't just buy any ornament that takes my eye. Thankfully, we've figured out ways to get chores done with minimal hassle now, and with the help of generous friends and campsite owners, we get hot baths often enough.
8580:
Transcription

DEB: It takes time, though, going to laundrettes instead of just throwing things in the washing machine, going to supermarkets more often because you can only store so much in your tiny fridge. If you think life on the road will free up your time, think again! But it is nice waking up to the sound of birds and having your day-to-day life affected so closely by the weather and seasons. You don't get that in the flat. If only we could travel to the places we wanted to, like Scotland or the Irish coast, and really see the country. That would be fantastic.

AIDEN: I was thirteen years old when I took a flight to London with my mum. Neither of us had been on a plane before, so we were excited but nervous. We knew that we had to get to the airport three hours before our flight took off, but what we thought was the check-in time was actually the departure time, so when we arrived at the airport, the flight was already boarding! The lady told us not to worry; we wouldn't miss our flight. But there were only two seats left, one in the middle and one at the back. We were so disappointed. I didn't want to sit away from my mum because I was nervous about flying, and she wanted to sit with me because she doesn't speak English. The lady must have seen my face because she said, 'Don't worry, I can sit you together.' She printed out our boarding cards and we ran to the gate. When we boarded, we turned towards economy class and the flight attendant told us we were going the wrong way. The lady at the desk had put us in business class so that we could sit together! It was so comfortable, and we got all kinds of extra treats! I only wish I'd realised sooner, and had thanked that lady properly.

EMILY: When I was 21, I took a flight to the US to spend some time with my boyfriend. When my dad dropped me off at the airport, he went into full parenting mode, fussing and worrying over me. He told the man at check-in that I'd only been on short flights before. The crew member told him not to worry and that I'd be well looked after, and he told me to wait on some chairs near security. I did so, and a bit later, I was escorted onto the plane in a car. I was the first on the plane and I saw that there was a colouring pack on my seat, which I thought was a bit odd. I was about to ask a cabin crew member about it, but they were busy with the other passengers who were all queuing and boarding after being cramped on a coach. A bit later, I was asked if I wanted to go up to the cockpit to see the pilot and I did. It was there that the captain asked me how old I was. He got a bit of a surprise when I told him. That's when I realised that my dad had made them think I needed special treatment as a minor. It was hilarious!

MICHAEL: I was on a flight from India to the USA with a stopover in Dubai. I was just boarding when I saw someone I recognized, but he was in a wheelchair, which was odd because I had always known him as a fit and healthy guy. It was curious, but I didn't know him well, so I decided not to get into conversation with him. He might not be in the mood for small talk if he was under the weather. I didn't see him during the flight; I think he was in first class. At Dubai, I saw him again being wheeled through security while I was queuing up, and then I saw him again after we arrived, and that's when he noticed me and gave me a cheery wave. It was about a week later when I saw him in the park. I couldn't believe my eyes. He was jogging! I couldn't understand how he'd made such a fast recovery. Anyway, he spotted me and jogged up to me, and we got chatting. It turned out that there was no injury at all. He'd just bought himself a fake doctor's certificate so that he could pass as a wheelchair passenger and get special treatment. Apparently, it's common practice!

You're probably thinking I wanted to get fit so I could look good and attract a new partner, but that wasn't it at all. NARRATOR: Maybe it's time to get rid of your ex's plush toy or their broken sunglasses, and maybe their lock of hair. Luckily, in Zagreb, Croatia, a place exists where these items can be preserved instead of just sitting at the back of your closet. Dražen Grubišić and Olinka Vištica, the founders of the museum, had this exact problem.
OLINKA: Dražen and myself first first met 20 years ago. He was a sculptor, artist, doing the clubs often, and I was at the time working with a French choreographer.
DRAZEN: Our relationship was great. We had a lot in common; we were quite busy at the time as well, so we traveled a lot, which was really nice. Yeah, it was a nice relationship.
OLINKA: Maybe work was taking over me. I was very ambitious at the time.
DRAZEN: It wasn't a spectacular breakup. It was more like, "Yeah, let's just split."
9714:
Transcription

OLINKA: There was this banal bunny. We would take it to different places when we would travel without the partners. And that was the trigger for us to think, "Okay, who takes the bunny?"
DRAZEN: We were sitting in a kitchen and talking about it, and it was fascinating that something so banal could have such a huge emotional trigger. To anybody else, it was just a banal object, but to you, it was like, you just look at it, and it's heart-wrenching. That's where the idea of the museum came about.
9715:
Transcription

NARRATOR: So, what makes an item worthy of a spot on a plinth?
OLINKA: There are no criteria you have to meet to be accepted as a part of the collection because I think it's the most beautiful thing, you become part of a huge community across the world with people you don't even know. But we all share this human connection through love, and its disappearance.
DRAZEN: All the descriptions are written by donors, so whoever gives the object is the one behind the story. I was kind of afraid at the beginning. You have no control over it, so I thought it might be boring or repetitive. And it turned out from the start, they write so well, and you have sometimes these really short three or four-sentence stories that give you like the insight and you want to know more. And they're like the trailer to movies that you want to see. As every other serious museum, we also have a gift shop with t-shirts, bags, chocolates, and so on. But they all have a quirky message dealing with the museum, dealing with break up, love. The most popular item is the big eraser. It's called Bad Memories Eraser. People usually, when they see it, start laughing and they get like - "Oh, I know who this goes to."
9716:
Transcription

NARRATOR: Does it ever get weird working with your ex?
OLINKA: It's a long process of 15 years learning how to work together, respect each other. That's the best thing you can do, to create something with someone, and to learn how to respect yourself and the other person in the process
DRAZEN: And prove that it's possible!
9717:
Transcription

DRAZEN: And prove that it's possible! Enabling people to get rid of these reminders and actually transform them into something else. The process of writing this story, packing the object, and sending it away, I'm sure, provides relief. And we've heard it from so many people.
NARRATOR: And this museum isn't just a quirky way to spend an afternoon in Zagreb.
OLINKA: Visitors empathize so much with other people. They learn how to overcome their own prejudices we all have, on some level, through this experience, which is for all of us the same.

PHIL: Westmarsh Footpaths Society, Phil speaking.
EMMA: Oh, hi, I got your phone number off the website, and I was wondering if I could join. I know I can do that on the website too, but I had a couple of questions.
PHIL: Sure, fire away.
EMMA: Well, I’ve walked with the Ramblers before, but I find their walks a bit challenging. They’re quite long and.. um, strenuous. Can you tell me about your walks?
PHIL: Of course. We actually have three types of walks. Our long walks aren’t that long—usually around eight miles, starting at 10 am... well, we meet half an hour before, so the walk leader can get everyone organised... and we’re usually finished at around 2, 2.30.
EMMA: I’m not sure I’m up to 8 miles yet...
PHIL: Well our short walks are around 4-6 miles, and they are usually at a moderate pace. It’s about being out enjoying the countryside, not getting there as fast as possible.
EMMA: Good. That sounds like my kind of walk!
PHIL: Great. We also have something called a leisure walk. We only started those this year and they are very popular with our older members. Our oldest walker is 92. Older members still want to walk, but can’t manage rough ground, steep hills or stiles, so we do 2-3 miles over easy ground – hence the leisure walk, They’re really popular.
EMMA: Wow! What a great idea. I think my mum would like that. Do you stop at a pub or something for lunch?
PHIL: No, we take a packed lunch, then we’re not tied as to where we can walk. Long and short walkers stop somewhere on the way, and leisure walkers have a picnic at the end of the walk because they start at 11 and the walk is usually only an hour, hour and a half, so.... everyone has a packed lunch.
EMMA: Right. That makes sense. Which day are the walks on, or does it vary?
PHIL: It does. We don’t walk at weekends. But if it’s Monday this week, it’ll be Tuesday next week and so on. It’s so people who are doing other things have a chance to join in at least some of the programme.
EMMA: That’s a great idea. And I look on the website for when the walks are?
PHIL: Yes, there’s a members’ area where you can see a walks calendar saying the days of the walks, the meeting point—usually a carpark or a landmark like a church—and the name and number of the walk leader in case you have any questions. But we also email the walks calendar out to members and send a weekly email to remind them of the walks the following week.
